questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of Herzberg's two-factor theory?
options: Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction, while motivators create genuine motivation
Workers are motivated only by money
Workers have five levels of need in a fixed order
Workers are motivated mainly by social interaction
questions.why: Herzberg found two separate scales. Fixing pay and conditions moves you from dissatisfied to neutral; only achievement, recognition, responsibility, the work itself and advancement create motivation.
whyNot: That is Taylor's scientific management.
That is Maslow's hierarchy of needs.
That is Mayo's human relations theory.

questions.stem: According to Herzberg, which of these is a motivator rather than a hygiene factor?
options: Responsibility
Pay
Working conditions
Company policy
questions.why: Responsibility is on Herzberg's motivator list, alongside achievement, recognition, the work itself and advancement.
whyNot: Pay is the classic hygiene factor: get it wrong and people are dissatisfied, get it right and they are simply not dissatisfied.
Conditions are a hygiene factor.
Company policy is a hygiene factor.

questions.stem: Which theory argues that workers are motivated mainly by money, so pay should be linked to output?
options: Taylor's scientific management
Mayo's human relations theory
Herzberg's two-factor theory
Maslow's hierarchy of needs
questions.why: Taylor broke jobs into simple repeated tasks and paid per unit produced. It survives today as piecework, commission and per-job gig work.
whyNot: Mayo argued for social needs: attention, teamwork and consultation.
Herzberg argued that pay only prevents dissatisfaction.
Maslow set out five levels of need, of which pay addresses mainly the lowest.

questions.stem: Which term is defined as: giving an employee more challenging and responsible tasks so the work itself becomes more rewarding?
options: Job enrichment
Job enlargement
Job rotation
Delegation
questions.why: Enrichment goes deeper: more responsibility. It is the method that matches Herzberg's motivators, which is why it is the most powerful of the three job methods.
whyNot: Enlargement is wider: more tasks at the same level of responsibility.
Rotation is sideways: different tasks at the same level, to reduce boredom.
Delegation passes a specific task and its authority down, which is related but narrower.

questions.stem: What is the difference between job enrichment and job enlargement?
options: Enrichment adds responsibility; enlargement adds more tasks at the same level
Enrichment adds more tasks; enlargement adds responsibility
They are two words for the same thing
Enrichment applies to managers only
questions.why: Deeper against wider. Only enrichment adds responsibility, so only enrichment is a Herzberg motivator. Enlargement done badly is simply more work, and employees notice.
whyNot: This reverses the two.
They are distinct and the distinction is regularly examined.
Both can apply at any level.

questions.stem: A business has well-paid but bored staff with high turnover. Which approach does Herzberg suggest?
options: Enrich the jobs, because more pay would not address the problem
Increase pay further
Improve the staff canteen
Introduce stricter supervision
questions.why: Pay is a hygiene factor, and it is already adequate, so more of it buys nothing. Boredom is a lack of motivators, which means changing the work itself through added responsibility and challenge.
whyNot: Adding to a hygiene factor that is already satisfactory does not create motivation.
Also a hygiene factor, and not the binding constraint here.
Supervision is a hygiene factor, and tightening it would probably make things worse.

questions.stem: Why is piecework usually unsuitable for a service business?
options: It rewards volume, while service is judged on quality
It is illegal in service industries
Service businesses have no measurable output
It always costs more than a fixed salary
questions.why: Paying per unit gives staff every incentive to rush. In a service business where the interaction is the product, speed at the expense of care damages the thing being sold.
whyNot: It is not illegal, merely poorly suited.
Output can often be measured, for example covers served. The problem is that the measure ignores quality.
The cost depends on rates and output, not on the method itself.

questions.stem: According to Maslow, why might offering recognition fail to motivate a very low-paid employee?
options: Lower needs must be met before higher ones motivate
Recognition is never motivating
Low-paid employees do not want recognition
Recognition is a hygiene factor
questions.why: Maslow's practical use is diagnostic: find the unmet level and act there. Esteem needs do not motivate someone whose physiological and safety needs are unmet.
whyNot: Recognition is motivating, once lower needs are satisfied.
An assumption about people rather than what the theory says.
Recognition is a Herzberg MOTIVATOR. This question is about Maslow in any case.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of empowerment?
options: Giving employees the authority to make decisions about their own work
Giving employees more tasks to do
Paying employees a share of profits
Moving employees between different tasks
questions.why: Empowerment is ongoing authority over your own work, which is strongly motivating. It needs training and clear boundaries to work.
whyNot: That is job enlargement.
That is profit share, a financial method.
That is job rotation.

questions.stem: What is the main weakness of profit share as a motivator?
options: An individual's effort is barely visible in the total, so the link is weak
It is illegal in most countries
It costs the business nothing
It only applies to managers
questions.why: Motivation depends on a clear link between effort and reward. In a large business, one person's extra effort changes total profit imperceptibly, so the incentive is diluted.
whyNot: Profit sharing is a common and legal practice.
It costs a share of profit, which is a real cost.
It can be offered at any level, and often is offered to all staff.

questions.stem: Which chain of reasoning best links motivation to business performance?
options: Motivation rises, so productivity rises and turnover falls, so unit costs fall and service improves, so the business is more competitive
Motivation rises, so profit rises
Motivation rises, so pay rises
Motivation rises, so the business grows
questions.why: It runs through two routes at once, cost and revenue, and states each link. Naming both routes is stronger than naming one, and the intermediate steps are where the analysis marks are.
whyNot: Only two links, with the whole mechanism missing.
Pay is an input to motivation, not a result of it.
A conclusion with no reasoning between the cause and the effect.

questions.stem: What is the most important limitation of using Taylor, Mayo, Maslow and Herzberg in an exam answer?
options: They are old, were tested on narrow groups, and are a guide rather than a formula
They have all been proven completely wrong
They only apply to manufacturing businesses
They cannot be used in a written answer
questions.why: All four come from specific studies decades ago, mostly of particular workforces. They remain useful frameworks, and treating them as laws that apply identically to every workforce is the error.
whyNot: They are still widely taught and used because they hold up broadly.
Herzberg and Maslow are applied across every sector including services.
Applying one of them properly is exactly what the higher marks reward.

questions.stem: Why is consulting employees and then ignoring their answer worse than not consulting at all?
options: It destroys trust, so future involvement is seen as a pretence
Consultation is legally binding
It costs more than a pay rise
Employees cannot tell the difference
questions.why: Mayo's point is that being genuinely involved motivates. A consultation that changes nothing signals that their views do not matter, which is more demotivating than never having been asked.
whyNot: Consultation is not generally binding, which is precisely why the trust matters.
Consultation is cheap. The cost here is trust, not money.
Employees notice very quickly when a decision was already made.

questions.stem: A business introduces performance-related pay. What is the most likely unintended consequence?
options: Teamwork suffers, as staff focus on their own measured targets
Staff stop coming to work
The wage bill becomes fixed
Productivity necessarily falls
questions.why: Individual targets make individual performance the priority, so helping a colleague becomes a cost to you. It also needs targets that are fair and measurable, which is harder than it sounds.
whyNot: An extreme claim with no basis.
Performance-related pay makes part of the wage bill variable, not fixed.
It usually raises measured productivity. The problem is what it does to everything not measured.
